name: Strange Attractors

lumenary.blurb: Four numbers, one tiny formula, repeated without end. The point never repeats itself and never leaves a narrow band, and the band breathes as the numbers drift.

facts.bestOn: Colourful pictures, which tint the cloud

why: A strange attractor is the shape drawn by a point that follows a simple rule for ever. The point never repeats and never escapes, and two points that start close together move apart quickly, which is the sign of chaos, yet both stay on the same fine, filamented set. A tiny change in four numbers gives a completely different picture.
how: Use one of two maps: Clifford’s x′ = sin(a y) + c cos(a x), y′ = sin(b x) + d cos(b y), or Peter de Jong’s x′ = sin(a y) − cos(b x), y′ = sin(c x) − cos(d y).
Each frame follow 48 points for 1,100 steps each.
Add every landing to a density histogram half the size of the picture.
Dim the histogram each frame by the linger factor, so the image is a running average that shows a glowing cloud.
Let the four numbers drift slowly, so the attractor breathes, and tint it from the picture.
history: Edward Lorenz found chaos in a weather model in 1963, and Michel Hénon published his map in 1976. Peter de Jong’s and Clifford Pickover’s maps became popular in the 1980s and 1990s, especially through Pickover’s books on computers, pattern and chaos. Strange attractors now appear in studies of weather, circuits, heartbeats and population dynamics.
uses: Studying chaos in weather, circuits and populations
Teaching sensitive dependence on initial conditions
terms: A set that a system settles into over time.
Extreme sensitivity to starting conditions, in a rule that is not random.
A count of how often each position was visited.
paragraphs: A strange attractor is the shape drawn by a point that follows a simple rule forever: the point never repeats and never escapes, and nearby starting points move apart exponentially (the sign of chaos) while still staying on one fine, filamented set. Two such maps are used. Clifford’s is x′ = sin(a y) + c cos(a x), y′ = sin(b x) + d cos(b y); Peter de Jong’s is x′ = sin(a y) − cos(b x), y′ = sin(c x) − cos(d y). A small change in the four numbers a, b, c and d gives a completely different picture, and three sets that are known to make good pictures are provided for each map.

Each frame 48 points are followed for 1,100 steps each, and every landing is added to a density histogram the size of half the picture. The histogram is dimmed by the linger factor on every frame, so the image is a running average that shows the attractor as a glowing cloud. Because |x′| and |y′| cannot be bigger than 1 + |c| and 1 + |d| for Clifford (and 2 for de Jong), the picture is scaled to fit those bounds exactly. The four numbers drift in time, each by a sine of its own speed and an amount set by the drift slider (up to 0.22), so the attractor breathes; the pointer adds up to ±0.3 to a and b. The brightness is a log-density tone map, and either a flame ramp or the picture’s own colours (each cell’s average) give the colour.

equations.note: The drifting parameters: δ is the drift slider, p the pointer position (the pointer acts on a and b only).
The log-density tone map: n is the number of landings in a cell and G the glow slider.

presets.text: De Jong gives silkier, more symmetric clouds.
A strong drift makes the attractor morph quickly.
The ember palette gives a fiery glow.
